newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM's brother triggers rice policy debate.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM's brother triggers rice policy debate.

text.p: A statement by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's brother criticising government policy on rice production has put him at the centre of a long-running debate over a food the Japanese consider sacred.

The premier's younger brother, Daijiro Hashimoto, who is governor of the prefecture of Kochi, said in his New Year's message that his government is unwilling to cooperate with the Agriculture Ministry in moves to reduce rice production.
Japan has been trying to reduce production of its long-time staple since the 1970s when prosperity and increased imports brought greater variety to the diet.

Japan's rice demand has fallen steadily, dropping from 13.41 million tonnes in 1963 to 10.02 million in 1994. Annual consumption per person has fallen in half to 66 kg (145 lbs), according to Agriculture Ministry data.
Last December, the ministry decided to set aside 787,000 hectares of rice paddy during fiscal 1997/98 ending March 31.

"We understand how painfully rice farmers feel the production controls. But without them, domestic rice prices are expected to fall further, which is also bad news for rice producers," a ministry official said.
"As long as there's a rice surplus, we're required to control rice production and need cooperation from local prefectural governments," he said.
In an interview with Reuters, Hashimoto said that he had not condemned the policy of his brother's administration.
"I'm not saying that Japan's set-aside policy for rice production makes no sense at all," he said.
But he added that the current system gives the government too much control.
"I think local farmers should decide on rice production controls on their own initiative, not by guidance by the government."
The Agriculture Ministry has estimated that domestic rice stocks at the end of last October stood at three million tonnes, almost double the 1.61 million tonnes of a year ago.
Good harvests in the past two years have swollen stocks in grain warehouses across the country. A stock level of 1.5 million tonnes is considered desirable throughout the year.
